one_liner: Julia's scalar Complex{Float64} Mandelbrot loop in the official Julia microbenchmarks; 1.46x faster than C in 2018 data, a tie today.
what_it_does: julia/perf.jl defines mandel(z) (escape-time loop, maxiter 80, z = z^2 + c on Complex{Float64}) and builds a 21x26 matrix of iteration counts with a comprehension over -2.0:0.1:0.5 by -1.0:0.1:1.0, checked against a sum of 14791; c/perf.c does the same with C99 double complex and a malloc'd int array. It is one of eight cross-language microbenchmarks the Julia project uses for the julialang.org performance chart, not a library: the takeaway is that idiomatic Julia complex arithmetic in a plain loop compiles to code on par with C.
how_it_is_fast: No special technique: Julia type-infers the loop to Complex{Float64}, inlines z^2 into a plain (ac - bd, ad + bc) multiply, and LLVM emits a scalar loop for the host CPU after JIT compilation (excluded from timing). The source gives no reason for the 2018 gap. In the 2018 table C was slower than every compiled language on this row (Julia 0.687, Fortran 0.702, Rust 0.751, Go 0.778 of C time, derived), which fits the verifier's reading that gcc 7.3.1's C99 Annex G complex multiply (NaN check with a __muldc3 fallback) cost C time. The same C source ties Julia when built with gcc 13.3.0, so that cost was specific to the old toolchain or CPU.
when_to_use: As evidence that scalar complex-number loops written naturally in Julia (Complex{Float64}, z^2 + c, array comprehension) run at C speed, so such kernels need not be rewritten in C.
When prototyping small numeric kernels (iteration counts, escape-time fractals, per-point complex maps) where JIT warm-up is paid once and the kernel runs many times.
As a ready harness (Makefile plus GitHub Actions workflow) to compare Julia against C, Fortran, Rust, Go, Swift and others on your own machine, with the identical algorithm in every language.
when_not_to_use: As proof that Julia is 1.46x faster than C: the project's current CI page (generated 2026-04-21, GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, gcc 13.3.0 -O2, Julia 1.12.6) has C 0.045061 ms vs Julia 0.045765 ms (Julia 1.016x of C time), and a 2022 CI run posted in issue #48 had C 0.08167 vs Julia 0.0796.

As evidence across the suite: in the current data Julia is behind C on all eight benchmarks (from 1.016x on mandelbrot and 1.03x on BLAS matmul to 3.1x on recursive fibonacci, derived from page data).
When you need a faster Mandelbrot than scalar C: neither side vectorizes across points, so explicit SIMD or GPU code is the lever, not the language.
For one-shot or start-up-sensitive runs: the timings exclude Julia start-up and the JIT compilation of mandel and the comprehension.
With -ffast-math expectations: neither the C build (no -ffast-math, -fcx-limited-range or -march) nor Julia uses relaxed floating point, so this row says nothing about fast-math code.

integration.form: source-drop (benchmark script julia/perf.jl; the mandelbrot part is about 20 lines)
integration.dependencies: none for the mandelbrot kernel (Base Julia); the full suite needs OpenBLAS, dSFMT 2.2.4 for C, and Test, Printf, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra stdlibs
integration.min_toolchain: Julia 1.0 for the 2018 data (perf.jl then used Compat); current perf.jl runs on Julia 1.x ('v1' in CI, 1.12.6 in the 2026-04-21 run); C side gcc -std=c99
integration.platforms: any Julia platform; published numbers are x86-64 only (i7-3960X for 2018 per julialang.org snippet, GitHub Actions runners now)
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (serial single-core benchmark; CI sets JULIA_NUM_THREADS=1)

gotchas: The 2018 harness was not symmetric: C timed 100 back-to-back mandelperf() calls per sample and divided by 100, kept the best over -O0..-O3 builds and 5 runs each, while Julia's old perfutil.jl @timeit timed single calls in a loop until at least 5 trials and 2000 ms had accumulated and reported the minimum single call. Issue #10 (2018-05-21) flagged the differing repetition counts and sum/assert inclusion; PR #100 (2026-03-02) standardized every language to one call per timed sample.
The 1.46x does not reproduce in the project's own current data (C 0.045061 vs Julia 0.045765 ms on 2026-04-21), so the win is a property of the 2018 toolchain, CPU or harness, not of Julia codegen.

The verifier's tie-breaker (gfortran on the same gcc matched Julia in 2018) does not hold today: gfortran 13.3.0 is 1.18x slower than C on this row in the 2026 data (0.05296 ms), and the Fortran mandelperf does less work (it sums into a volatile scalar instead of filling an array).

bin/benchmarks.csv (Julia 1.0-era data, added in 2022 by #65) carries no versions or hardware; gcc 7.3.1, Julia 1.0.0 and the i7-3960X come only from the julialang.org/benchmarks page. Julia's Make.inc v1.0.0 defines JCFLAGS, not CFLAGS, and adds -march only when MARCH is set, so the C build most likely had no -march.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Its Fortran twin (same suite, 1.42x in the same 2018 table) shares every caveat here, and the Mojo SIMD Mandelbrot sibling is an explicit vectorization win against scalar C rather than a like-for-like comparison. Cite this entry only for 'Julia's scalar complex loop matches C'; for a measured win, look elsewhere in the catalog.
verified_claims_summary: In the Julia 1.0-era bin/benchmarks.csv, userfunc_mandelbrot took 0.076702 ms in C (gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99, best of -O0..-O3, 100-call averages) and 0.052706 ms in Julia (minimum single call), about 1.46x faster, on an i7-3960X per julialang.org. The project's current GitHub Actions run (gcc 13.3.0 -O2, Julia 1.12.6, one call per sample for all languages) shows a tie: C 0.045061 ms, Julia 0.045765 ms.
status_note: Actively maintained by the Julia project (MIT; CI restructured in March 2026, results page rebuilt 2026-04-21), but its own current data shows parity with C on this row, so the catalogued 1.46x is a historical 2018 result that should be read as at best a tie.
